summary: This standards-track memo defines the command codes and attributes (AVPs) needed to carry EAP packets between a network access server and a back-end authentication server using Diameter. This lets a network access server pass EAP authentication on to a central server.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a network, a gatekeeper asks a central server to check your identity. This document defines the messages they use to pass your login proof.

subtitle: How a network access server hands EAP authentication to a back-end Diameter server and gets the verdict and keys back.

tldr.problem: EAP supports many authentication methods, but a network access server (NAS) that sits between a user and the network usually cannot judge them itself. It needs a standard way to pass EAP packets to a central server that can.
tldr.mechanism: The Diameter EAP application defines the Diameter-EAP-Request and Diameter-EAP-Answer commands (Command-Code 268) and new AVPs, chiefly EAP-Payload, so the NAS can wrap EAP packets, relay them to the home server and receive the result and keying material.
tldr.outcome: A NAS can pass EAP through to the home Diameter server, with rules for proxies, retransmission, accounting and translation to and from RADIUS. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 7268 and RFC 8044.

today: RFC 4072 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7268 and RFC 8044, so read it together with those documents. It remains the base specification of the Diameter EAP application.

sections.title: Carrying EAP over Diameter
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is an authentication framework that supports multiple authentication mechanisms on dedicated links, switched circuits, and wired and wireless links. This RFC specifies the Diameter EAP application, which carries EAP packets between a Network Access Server (NAS) acting as an EAP authenticator and a back-end authentication server.

It builds on the Diameter Network Access Server Application (NASREQ, RFC 4005) and is meant for similar environments. It defines new Command-Codes and Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs), can be used alongside NASREQ (chosen by whether the user authenticates with EAP or PAP/CHAP), and can work together with RADIUS EAP support (RFC 3579).

Authentication runs end to end between the EAP client and its home Diameter server, which reduces the room for fraud such as replay and man-in-the-middle attacks and makes mutual authentication possible, something PAP and CHAP cannot do in a roaming PPP environment.
sections.plainLanguage: The gatekeeper (the NAS) just carries your answers to the central office in an envelope. The office decides whether you may come in.

sections.title: How an EAP Exchange Flows
sections.content:
Nodes advertise support by including the Diameter EAP Application ID value 5 in the Auth-Application-Id AVP of the capabilities exchange. If a NAS gets DIAMETER_APPLICATION_UNSUPPORTED, the home server does not support EAP, and the NAS MAY try another method such as PAP or CHAP, with caution because this could be a downgrade attack.

Once EAP starts on the link, the NAS typically sends a Diameter-EAP-Request with an empty EAP-Payload AVP, meaning EAP-Start. The server answers with a Diameter-EAP-Answer carrying an EAP packet in EAP-Payload and the Result-Code DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH, which says another request is expected. A preferred approach is for the NAS to send the EAP-Request/Identity itself and forward the EAP-Response/Identity in the first request, saving round trips; the NAS SHOULD then copy the identity into a User-Name AVP, which roaming needs for routing.

The exchange ends when the server sends a Result-Code for success or failure. The NAS uses the Result-Code, and MUST NOT rely on the contents of the optional EAP-Payload, to decide whether to give service. A successful answer SHOULD carry the authorization AVPs if authorization was requested, and MAY carry an EAP-Master-Session-Key AVP with keying material for protecting traffic between the user and the NAS. The home server MAY ask for re-authentication with Re-Auth-Request. If a server fails mid-session, an alternate server may be used but the authentication must restart from the beginning.
sections.plainLanguage: The gatekeeper asks the office, "who is this?", relays the questions back and forth, and finally the office says yes or no. The gatekeeper only goes by that yes or no.

sections.title: Four Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Diameter's IPsec and TLS protect messages hop by hop, and no end-to-end NAS-to-home-server mechanism exists, so the RFC lists four example scenarios, not exhaustive and combinable, for how to protect the messages that may carry the master session key.

  • Direct connection: the NAS talks to the home server, which supplies all authorization AVPs and keying material. The RFC says this is the most likely scenario for small networks.
  • Redirects: the NAS asks a redirect agent for the home server (Redirect-Host and Redirect-Host-Usage), then proceeds as before. Knowledge of realms and home servers is centralized, so the NAS needs no change when, for example, a new roaming agreement is made.
  • Direct EAP, authorization via agents: EAP is done with the home server using Auth-Request-Type AUTHENTICATE_ONLY, and authorization AVPs come from local proxy agents with a separate NASREQ AA-Request of type AUTHORIZE_ONLY, for when the home server cannot supply them all.
  • Proxy agents: as the first scenario, but through proxies. The proxies can see the EAP session keys, so this is not suitable where proxies cannot be trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: The gatekeeper can phone the central office directly, ask a receptionist which office to call, get a second office to fill in extra details, or go through middlemen. Middlemen can overhear secrets, so only use ones you trust.

sections.title: The DER and DEA Commands
sections.content:
The application defines one command pair, both with Command-Code 268. The Diameter-EAP-Request (DER) has the 'R' bit set, goes from the Diameter client to the server, and conveys an EAP-Response from the EAP client. It MUST contain one EAP-Payload AVP; an empty one MAY start a session. A later DER in a multi-round exchange MUST repeat any State AVPs from the preceding answer.

The Diameter-EAP-Answer (DEA) has the 'R' bit cleared and is sent for one of three reasons: the exchange needs another request (Result-Code DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH); the client was authenticated and authorized, in which case the message MUST show success, SHOULD carry an EAP-Success payload, and MUST cause the NAS to provide service; or authentication or authorization failed, where an EAP-Payload SHOULD be included but is not used to decide on service. A successful answer to a request for authorization MUST include the relevant authorization AVPs.

Both commands carry the usual Diameter header AVPs (Session-Id, Auth-Application-Id, Origin-Host, Origin-Realm, Auth-Request-Type) plus many NASREQ AVPs. For AA-Request and AA-Answer used in the authorization-only scenario, Application Identifier 1 (NASREQ) is used; accounting commands use 3 and the others use 0.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two envelopes: one the gatekeeper sends to ask, and one the office sends back with its reply. Both are numbered 268.

sections.title: The New AVPs
sections.content:
An AVP is a labeled field in a Diameter message. The RFC defines four new ones with Diameter codes, plus one RADIUS-style attribute:

  • EAP-Payload (462, OctetString) encapsulates the EAP packet exchanged between the EAP client and the home server.
  • EAP-Reissued-Payload (463, OctetString) carries the previous EAP Request again after a non-fatal error.
  • EAP-Master-Session-Key (464, OctetString) holds keying material for protecting traffic between user and NAS. How it is used depends on the link layer and is out of scope.
  • Accounting-EAP-Auth-Method (465, Unsigned64) names the EAP method used. For expanded types it holds (Vendor-Id * 2^32) + Vendor-Type.
  • EAP-Key-Name (RADIUS attribute type 102, OctetString) is an opaque key identifier generated by the EAP method. A NAS MUST send it empty in a request, and a server MUST silently discard it if non-empty.

For accounting, the NAS MAY include Accounting-Auth-Method with value 5 (EAP) in Accounting-Requests, and one or more Accounting-EAP-Auth-Method AVPs MAY name the method(s). A server that authenticated the user SHOULD include them in a successful answer so the NAS can pass them on. The RFC also gives occurrence tables listing which AVPs may appear in DER and DEA.
sections.plainLanguage: An AVP is a labeled box inside the envelope. This memo adds boxes for the login packet, the secret key, the name of the key, and a note saying how you proved who you are.

sections.title: Invalid Packets, Retransmission and Fragmentation
sections.content:
As a pass-through, the NAS MUST validate the EAP header fields (Code, Identifier, Length) before forwarding in either direction. Responses must carry Code 2 and match the current Identifier; requests from the server must carry Code 1. Mismatching pending Responses are silently discarded. The NAS does not check EAP method fields, so an invalid packet can still get through.

A server that does not understand an EAP-Payload decides from the EAP Type whether the error is fatal. A fatal error MUST get an answer with a failure Result-Code and an EAP Failure payload. A non-fatal error MUST get DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH with no EAP-Payload but with an EAP-Reissued-Payload holding the previous EAP Request, and the NAS then retries or resends the previous request. To limit denial of service, the NAS should keep a finite buffer for EAP packets from the peer, and the server should allow only a modest number of invalid packets per session before ending it with DIAMETER_AUTHENTICATION_REJECTED. By default 5 is recommended.

For retransmission, the NAS retransmits lost EAP packets, and a Multi-Round-Time-Out AVP in an answer sets the retransmission timer for that Request alone; this helps with, for example, token cards. For fragmentation, the server cannot discover the link MTU, so a NAS may send a Framed-MTU AVP, and the server MUST NOT send an EAP-Payload longer than that value, allowing for the link type.
sections.plainLanguage: The gatekeeper checks that each note has the right stamp and number before passing it on. If the office gets a note it cannot read, it asks again, and after too many bad notes it ends the conversation.

sections.title: Translating To and From RADIUS
sections.content:
Translation agents bridge RADIUS and Diameter, following the NASREQ guidelines plus extras here. Going from RADIUS to Diameter, one or more EAP-Message attributes become a single EAP-Payload AVP (concatenated), and an empty EAP-Message of length 2 means EAP-Start and becomes an empty EAP-Payload.

In the other direction, EAP-Payload is split across EAP-Message attributes if needed. An EAP-Reissued-Payload becomes EAP-Message attributes plus a RADIUS Error-Cause attribute with value 202 (decimal), "Invalid EAP Packet (Ignored)". The Multi-Round-Time-Out AVP maps to the RADIUS Session-Timeout attribute. The EAP-Master-Session-Key can map to the vendor-specific MS-MPPE-Recv-Key and MS-MPPE-Send-Key attributes, the first up to 32 octets in the first and the next up to 32 in the second, as described in RFC 2548.

Accounting-EAP-Auth-Method AVPs are discarded when sent toward RADIUS, and the vendor-specific MS-Acct-EAP-Type attribute can map to and from that AVP; since it does not support expanded EAP types, values above 255 should be sent as 254.
sections.plainLanguage: Some offices speak an older language. A translator rewrites each envelope so both sides understand it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Diameter peer connections can be protected with IPsec or TLS, which the RFC believes sufficient under the normal Internet threat model. Authorization is also required: a server must decide whether a client may act as a NAS for the user, and a NAS must decide whether a server may act as home server for the realm. This matters especially with redirects, where a compromised agent could give the wrong home server address.

Compromised or abusive agents are a main concern. They can change the Result-Code to DIAMETER_SUCCESS to admit unauthorized users, or add AVPs for tunnels, routes, filters or callbacks. Some of this can be blocked by refusing certain AVPs or accepting them only from certain nodes. Agents also see the EAP-Master-Session-Key, so the RFC strongly recommends avoiding agents that cannot be trusted to keep keys secret.

Negotiation attacks that push a user to PAP or CHAP are reduced by a per-connection policy at the peer and a per-user policy at the server, and a NAS MUST attempt EAP for every session if any of its peers MUST do EAP. Messages can reveal user identity and approximate location, so identity-protecting EAP methods and pseudonyms help. A compromised NAS can also misstate its identity (such as SSID or BSSID) to the client even though its possession of the keys shows it is authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: Dishonest middlemen could say yes to the wrong person or peek at the secret key, so only trusted middlemen should be used.
